**Solution 1 (326) is correct; Solution 2 (210) is not.**

**Invariant.** Each operation turns exactly 3 white cells black, so the number of black cells is always 1 + 3k. A full board needs n² ≡ 1 (mod 3), so 3 ∤ n. This rules out every multiple of 3.

**Solution 2 is wrong.** Its induction step claims one operation turns a k×k black block into a (k+1)×(k+1) block. That only holds for k = 1. For k ≥ 2 the step needs 2k+1 new cells, and one operation colours only 3. It also contradicts the invariant, since it would make n = 3 possible.

**n = 5 is impossible.** The first two operations are forced:
- Op 1 must use the corner square, colouring (1,2), (2,1), (2,2).
- Op 2 must be the square at rows 2–3, columns 2–3, colouring (2,3), (3,2), (3,3).

The corner cell (5,1) can only be coloured by the square at rows 4–5, columns 1–2, and that operation needs exactly one black cell among (4,1), (4,2), (5,2).
- (4,1) can only be blackened by the square at rows 3–4, columns 1–2, which also blackens (4,2), so (4,1) can never be the lone black cell.
- (5,2) can only be blackened by the square at rows 4–5, columns 2–3, which also blackens (4,2) and leaves two black cells in the corner square, so (5,2) can never be the lone black cell.
- (4,2) can only be blackened first by the square at rows 3–4, columns 2–3. That square already has (3,2) and (3,3) black from Op 2, so it can never be used.

So (5,1) can never be coloured, and 5×5 is impossible.

**Consistency check.** I constructed a full colouring for n = 4 by hand. Excluding multiples of 3 and n = 5, the smallest 20 values are 1, 2, 4, 7, 8, 10, 11, 13, 14, 16, 17, 19, 20, 22, 23, 25, 26, 28, 29, 31. Their sum is 326, which matches Solution 1. I did not verify constructions for every such n (e.g. n = 7), so this rests on the mod-3 invariant, the n = 5 obstruction, and the n = 4 construction, plus Solution 1's claim that the remaining n work.

CHOICE: 1
